W7220891770.abstract: Endpoint accuracy on abstract-reasoning benchmarks does not reveal whether a language model has acquired a transferable rule or fit distribution-specific regularities. We study this distinction in small language models on the ARC-TGI benchmark, which organizes abstract grid transformations into controllable task families and supports resampling, spatial shifts, and cross-benchmark transfer. Across more than 1,000 runs, we profile decoder-only, encoder--decoder, and mixture-of-experts model families under supervised fine-tuning. We examine the efficiency and stability of skill acquisition, robustness beyond the training distribution, interactions with model family and task formulation, and layer-wise attention signatures that accompany behavioral differences. Substantial in-distribution accuracy is attainable, but acquisition is sensitive to optimization and unevenly distributed across task families. Performance deteriorates sharply outside the training distribution, including when the rule is retained but grid scale changes. Greater training-set depth and breadth yield uneven gains, while the effect of additional in-context examples depends on model family. Executable-rule induction also yields correct solutions not observed under direct grid generation. On selected tasks, attention diagnostics show distinct concentration and context-dependence profiles, but do not establish general causal mechanisms. Overall, abstract-reasoning scores are conditional on the model, adaptation regime, evaluation distribution, and response format.

W7220905223.abstract: Diffusion large language models dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive language models through bidirectional diffusion-based token generation. However, their growing model sizes and high inference costs make efficient deployment challenging: full-sequence denoising repeatedly invokes compute-intensive forward passes, while block-diffusion models additionally introduce a memory-intensive KV-cache. Low-bit weight-activation quantization is therefore attractive, yet existing dLLM post-training quantization methods rely on calibration data despite activation distributions shifting across masking states and denoising steps. We present SoloQ, a calibration-free quantization framework that maps weights and activations into a normalized rotated basis with a predictable marginal distribution, enabling data-independent quantization. SoloQ combines a structured K-RPBH rotation with a lightweight rescaling correction for calibration-free quantization. Its predictable post-rotation distribution supports both distribution-matched codebooks and hardware-native NVFP4. For block-diffusion models, SoloQ further applies commit-time KV-cache quantization to compress persistent states without perturbing the actively denoised block. Across full-sequence dLLMs (LLaDA and Dream) and block-diffusion dLLMs(Fast-dLLM v2 and Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion), SoloQ retains accuracy under 4-bit quantization and outperforms calibration-based baselines on knowledge- and reasoning-intensive benchmarks. With NVFP4, SoloQ reduces peak memory by up to 2.61X and accelerates end-to-end inference by up to 2.24X.

W7220957812.abstract: Refining user stories (USs) into tasks is an important step in agile software development, as it translates software requirements into project management artifacts that are assigned to team members. This story-to-task decomposition can be tedious. In this paper, we propose and evaluate DELTA, a Large Language Model (LLM)-based approach that automatically generates tasks from USs and assesses the quality of the resulting decompositions. We conduct a two-phase empirical study to evaluate DELTA. In the first phase, we identify the best-performing DELTA configuration by comparing different prompting strategies, LLM families, and sizes using text similarity metrics on human-created and LLM-generated decompositions. The comparison based on these metrics did not identify a single consistently best-performing configuration. Therefore, in the second phase, we conducted an expert evaluation to determine whether the observed differences in text similarity are reflected in expert judgments and whether DELTA’s criteria-based evaluation module, which uses LLM judges, aligns with expert judgments. Our results show that DELTA’s evaluation module produces rankings that align more closely with expert judgments than text similarity metrics. Moreover, experts generally prefer the top three LLM-generated decompositions, as ranked by LLM judges, over those created by humans, and they express a willingness to adopt DELTA.

W7221004467.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can solve many narrow tasks, but querying them separately for millions of related instances can be prohibitively expensive. Can LLM agents autonomously create cheaper solutions for such workloads? We call this ability "bottling": the ability to turn general capabilities into task-specific solutions that balance answer quality and amortised cost. We introduce BOTTLED, a benchmark in which agents receive an entire unlabelled workload and must complete it under fixed time, compute and LLM API budgets. Agents choose their own approach, such as training a small model or writing a reusable program. Across ten models and three tasks, we find that strong zero-shot task performance does not reliably translate into strong bottling capabilities. Models with similar zero-shot scores can differ substantially after bottling, and 48 of 60 bottling runs score below the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval of their model's zero-shot performance. Moreover, 31 of 60 runs underperform the stronger of two small-model distillation baselines with the same token budget. Nevertheless, bottling can yield substantial savings: on query-product relevance classification, Opus 5 retains about 82% of its zero-shot macro-F1 at roughly 657 times lower reported cost. Bottling is also competitive with Jev, a "system one" model built especially for cheap, repetitive inference: Opus 5 on the same task recovers about 94% of Jev's macro-F1 at a quarter of Jev's projected full-workload cost. BOTTLED provides a basis for evaluating and improving agents' ability to invest limited resources in reusable solutions for large, repetitive workloads.

W7221011081.abstract: This paper examines how autonomous agents are positioned when organizations connect language-model functions to operational systems, consumer services, and device-side resources. The analysis uses four illustrative cases: Hand Enterprise Solutions (HAND), China Mobile's Lingxi smart agent, Espressif, and Intretech. Evidence is drawn from academic research, public product documentation, annual reports, and company disclosures. The study retains a three-layer framework consisting of an enterprise-grade layer, a consumer-grade layer, and a technology-support layer. Enterprise-grade and consumer-grade agents are compared through strategic positioning, technical architecture, business model, and compliance requirements. The cases suggest that models, retrieval, memory, and tool invocation are shared components, but their operational implications vary with authority scope, system integration, device constraints, and the possible consequences of an incorrect action. Enterprise settings require clear roles, permission boundaries, records of agent actions, and review arrangements. Consumer services place greater weight on multimodal interaction, service routing, device linkage, and user authorization. The technology-support layer affects whether functions can remain on a device, be processed at the edge, or depend on cloud resources. This paper offers a qualitative cross-case analysis of deployment conditions. It does not estimate causal performance effects or rank the organizations discussed.

W7221104099.abstract: BACKGROUND: Artificial intelligence (AI) is now applied across the pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) pathway, yet the literature has grown faster than the evidence needed to act on it. The question is not whether an algorithm can predict an endpoint, but whether it yields information reliable, generalizable, and actionable enough to change a clinically meaningful decision. METHODS: In this narrative, in a non-systematic review of PDAC-specific literature, we grade applications on an author-defined evidence-readiness framework (development, internal, external, prospective validation, clinical impact, and implementation) and on four dimensions-validation, comparator, actionability, and impact. FINDINGS: Contemporary meta-analyses show high pooled accuracy for AI-based early detection and for distinguishing PDAC from mass-forming pancreatitis (sensitivity ~0.88-0.92, specificity ~0.90-0.93), but with extreme heterogeneity, low radiomics quality, scarce external validation, and-for electronic health-record risk models-positive predictive values often below 1% at population prevalence. Computed tomography (CT)-based detection and risk enrichment are among the more mature applications identified, yet none has been shown to improve stage distribution, resection rate, or survival. Treatment prediction is held to a strict standard, distinguishing prognostic association from a validated treatment-by-biomarker interaction. CONCLUSIONS: The rate-limiting steps are no longer algorithmic but translational-external and prospective validation, calibration, appropriate comparators, and workflow integration.

W7221503113.abstract: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), autonomous agents, and tool-using artificial intelligence has created new possibilities for automating significant portions of the scientific research lifecycle. Traditional scientific research generally requires researchers to independently conduct literature reviews, formulate hypotheses, design experiments, analyze data, and validate findings. Although artificial intelligence has increasingly supported individual stages of this process, most existing systems remain task-specific and require substantial human intervention. This paper proposes a multi-agent framework for autonomous scientific research in which specialized artificial intelligence agents collaboratively perform literature discovery, knowledge retrieval, hypothesis generation, experimental design, data analysis, critical evaluation, and validation. The proposed framework combines LLM-based reasoning with retrieval-augmented generation, external scientific databases, computational tools, experiment simulators, and verification agents. A central feature of the framework is the use of independent critic and validation agents to reduce hallucinations, unsupported hypotheses, methodological errors, and reproducibility problems. The proposed architecture follows a closed-loop research process in which hypotheses are generated from evidence, experiments are designed to test those hypotheses, results are analyzed, and conclusions are subjected to independent verification before being accepted. The paper further proposes an evaluation framework based on scientific validity, novelty, factuality, reproducibility, experimental efficiency, citation correctness, and human expert agreement. The framework provides a conceptual foundation for developing autonomous scientific research systems while maintaining human oversight at critical decision points. The study argues that agentic AI should not simply replace individual research tasks but should function as an auditable collaborative research ecosystem capable of supporting evidence-based scientific discovery.

W7221659290.abstract: Protein engineering has become a cornerstone of modern biotechnology and therapeutic development, enabling the design and optimization of proteins for applications ranging from biologics and vaccines to precision therapeutics. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have fundamentally transformed this field by accelerating protein structure prediction, function analysis, sequence optimization, and de novo protein design. This review provides an overview of the emerging role of AI in protein engineering and its implications for therapeutic development and precision medicine. Key AI-driven technologies, including machine learning, deep learning, protein language models, and generative AI, are discussed in the context of protein structure prediction, function prediction, and rational protein design. The review further examines the application of these technologies in therapeutic protein development, antibody engineering, vaccine design, immunotherapy, and AI-assisted drug discovery. Particular attention is given to the integration of AI with multi-omics technologies, which enables the identification of patient-specific molecular characteristics and supports the development of personalized therapeutic strategies. The convergence of AI, protein engineering, and precision medicine has created new opportunities for designing biologics tailored to individual disease mechanisms and patient profiles. Despite these advances, challenges related to data quality, model interpretability, experimental validation, ethical considerations, and regulatory oversight remain important barriers to widespread clinical implementation. Emerging technologies, including biological foundation models, generative AI systems, autonomous protein engineering platforms, and digital twin technologies, are expected to further expand the capabilities of AI-driven therapeutic design. Collectively, these developments position AI as a transformative force in protein engineering, accelerating therapeutic innovation and supporting the transition toward more precise, personalized, and effective healthcare solutions.

W7221690820.abstract: Agentic AI systems use language models to plan, select tools and act across multiple steps, which makes them attractive for enterprise workflows and also hazardous, because their output is a sequence of actions on systems of record rather than text for a person to read. This paper analyses how autonomous agents differ from conventional workflow automation and proposes the Governed Agentic Workflow Architecture (GAWA). GAWA comprises a staged execution pipeline with explicit validation, approval and audit stages; an orchestration model that places agents beneath a workflow engine; a six-requirement tool contract for interaction with enterprise systems; and a five-layer control stack covering policy, pre-action checks, execution controls, post-action validation and human decision. The architecture is evaluated qualitatively against six enterprise scenarios: invoice processing, document approval, customer requests, sales requests, knowledge retrieval and task routing. The paper also defines metrics for empirical evaluation. The findings indicate that appropriate autonomy should follow the consequence of an action rather than the sophistication of the task, and that most of the practical value arises when agents propose and route while deterministic checks and people retain control over irreversible effects

W7221759186.abstract: Abstract Large language models and agentic artificial intelligence provide the reasoning layer of autonomous aerial and ground robots, but the architectures remain fragmented across the two communities. This systematic review, reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 statement, searched ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, ProQuest, EBSCO, and Google Scholar from January 2020 through April 2026. Of 5298 records, 2228 remained after duplicates were removed and 124 studies were included: 67 aerial, 41 ground, and 16 on both platforms or a generic architecture. Six patterns appear, from a language model used only as a task-specific tool to an end-to-end foundation model, such as vision-language-action models. Open-loop pipelines, closed-loop pipelines, hierarchical executives, and multi-agent systems lie between those extremes. The model carries semantic reasoning, task decomposition, and tool orchestration, while classical planners and controllers retain trajectories, safety, and real-time control. Memory appears in 62 of 124 studies (50%) and function calling in 37 (30%), yet only 13 (10%) run the model onboard and 44 (35%) validate a physical robot. Aerial systems emphasize long-range vision and mission planning; ground systems emphasize local perception and interaction; both follow the same hybrid pattern. A suitability matrix shows that specialized vision models remain preferable for geometric perception. Designers should match the pattern to the task dynamics and choose the model for latency, safety, and where inference runs, rather than for benchmark score alone. Hallucination, spatial reasoning, inference latency, and the lack of standardized evaluation still limit deployment.

W7221762764.abstract: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models have emerged as powerful generative priors across domains ranging from molecular design to high-resolution image synthesis. However, standard diffusion sampling is inherently biased toward high-likelihood regions, often limiting the diversity of outputs. In many domains, a single, high-likelihood sample is insufficient. Instead, diverse portfolios of high-performing solutions are required, motivating methods that uncover a model's full expressive range. Here we show that integrating Quality-Diversity (QD) optimisation with diffusion models enables the discovery of diverse, high-performing outputs. We first propose Quality-Diversity Diffusion, a framework that adapts QD to diffusion models by directly optimising the model's latent noise and conditioning embeddings and leveraging embedding models to quantify diversity. Second, we introduce a novel h-space Spectral Mutation operator, which guides search along directions of maximal semantic sensitivity by analysing principal singular vectors of the model's input-to-activation Jacobian. We evaluate our combined approach, Spectral-Guided Quality-Diversity Diffusion, on text-to-image generation. Against 12 baselines, our method consistently achieves the lowest FID score, demonstrating an excellent balance of image quality and diversity.

W7221814326.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (LLM-MAS) use specialized agents that exchange messages to accomplish complex tasks. Their reliance on networked protocols, remote tools, and model endpoints exposes communication to message loss, delay, and context expiration. Because agents often exchange open-ended natural language, anomalies can alter task-relevant information while leaving messages processable, allowing semantic errors to propagate through subsequent interactions. Systematic studies of faults in inter-agent communication remain limited. This paper presents a large-scale empirical study of how communication faults manifest, propagate, and affect task outcomes in LLM-MAS. We construct a cross-layer taxonomy linking lower-stack disturbances to application-visible faults and develop a fault-injection and tracing pipeline. Our evaluation covers more than 29,000 executions across 100 tasks, five domains, three workflow topologies, and three model configurations. We find that 20.7% of failures with complete detection records occur without an immediate failure signal, reaching 76.2% for partial-content faults. Flat maintains 53.0% task success under communication faults, compared with 3.3% and 3.2% for Sequential and Hierarchical, respectively. This advantage primarily arises when an alternative information path preserves the evidence required by downstream agents. We also evaluate execution-side and evidence protection mechanisms and find that they recover different failure cases. Evidence recovery depends on whether trustworthy information remains accessible through an unaffected path. These observations provide empirical insights into communication-fault propagation, workflow resilience, and protection design for LLM-MAS.

W7221818204.abstract: Existing large language model (LLM) based multi-agent systems have been shown to scale poorly, and we identify three problems: reading burden that grows with the group, useful information diluted by shared work of unknown quality, and fragility to failed agents. We argue that the problems are largely due to agent-centric designs: the coordination structure is wired into fixed workflows, central coordinators, or peer-to-peer messaging, and recent blackboard-style methods that move the coordination into a shared medium relieve only the last problem. To close the gaps, we build ScaleMAS, where asynchronous agents interact with a shared datastore of linked messages via three operations: publishing messages with optional references to earlier ones that they build on, searching for messages by content, and visiting messages by address. Search returns at most $k$ messages, so an agent's read stays bounded at any group size; results are ranked by relevance and by how often they are cited, which we find to be an effective proxy for quality; and messages persist after their producers leave, so the group carries on when individual agents fail. Across four agentic tasks, ScaleMAS outperforms agent-centric and blackboard-style baselines at lower inference compute, continues to scale up to 128 agents, and tolerates losing agents midway.

W7221893052.abstract: The article is devoted to the problem of assessing the security of applications that function with the involvement of artificial intelligence agents. AI agents operate on the basis of large language models and perform tasks in the area of event log analysis, processing of technical documentation of the facility, and analysis of data in databases of a critical infrastructure facility. Agents can also be involved in monitoring tasks and interactions with SOC/SIEM platforms. Among the differences that make agentic applications potentially dangerous is the ability to autonomously call external applications and perform other intelligent actions that expand the attack surface. The risks include privilege escalation, confidential data leakage, and execution of actions that were not initially provided for by the security policy. The aim of the study is to develop a method for assessing the security of agentic applications, which is oriented toward application in critical infrastructure tasks. The method is suitable for comparative analysis of different versions of large language models and configurations of agentic applications. The method includes work with a threat model, a catalogue of test scenarios, and the proposed system of quantitative metrics. The functional part of the method consists of a procedure for automated testing and the formation of recommendations regarding the policy of differentiating agents’ access to data and tools. The threat model concerns the levels of the large language model and external tools, and takes into account the following categories of the most typical attacks: 1) direct prompt injection, 2) indirect prompt injection through external data, 3) tool misuse, 4) confidential data leakage, 5) privilege escalation. The Attack Success Rate (ASR) is used as an indicator for quantitative assessment, and additionally, the indicators of tool misuse, data leakage, and privilege escalation are used. The operability of the proposed method is shown experimentally, in an isolated software environment implemented in Python using LangChain and Ollama. The agent was tested using tools that simulated reading, writing, execution of SQL queries, data search, and sending messages. The experiments were carried out for the Llama 3.1 8B, Ministral 3 8B, and Qwen 3 8B models using 50 test scenarios and tenfold repetition of each scenario; the total volume of the experiment amounted to 2,000 runs. It was established that the vulnerabilities of the models differ significantly, and the most dangerous direction for all investigated LLMs is confidential data leakage, with the value of the corresponding indicator ranging from 20% to 70%. The use of the “thinking” mode in Qwen 3 made it possible to reduce the overall attack success rate from 22% to 6.2%. However, the use of this mode does not completely eliminate the risks of data leakage and unauthorized privilege escalation. The results of the study provide grounds to formulate recommendations: to apply the principle of least privilege, where possible to use read-only mode, and to necessarily involve a human operator to confirm the execution of critical operations. The proposed method can be used for comparative assessment and preliminary testing of agentic applications that are used in information and analytical tasks of critical infrastructure.

W7222752295.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable fluency but remain fundamentally unreliable for knowledge-intensive tasks due to hallucination, temporal staleness, and lack of verifiability.Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a dominant architectural paradigm that grounds generation in external evidence.This paper provides a comprehensive investigation into how RAG reshapes LLM reliability across factual accuracy, citation fidelity, temporal freshness, and robustness to noise.We benchmark five RAG variants against closed-book baselines using secondary datasets including Natural Questions, TriviaQA, HotpotQA, and RGB.Results show an average 23.7% reduction in hallucination rate and 31.2%improvement in citation grounding when using advanced retrieval with self-reflection.However, we identify critical failure modes: retriever-generator misalignment, context distraction, and over-reliance on irrelevant passages.We propose a reliability framework and demonstrate that corrective and modular RAG designs significantly mitigate these risks.Our findings establish RAG as necessary but not sufficient for trustworthy deployment.

W7222786903.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in consumer facing decision environments, where it supports or automates recommendations, credit assessment, personalised pricing, risk classification, digital contracting, and information filtering. This article examines AI driven consumer decision making from an integrated decision support, legal, and governance perspective. It analyses how opacity, autonomy, data dependence, algorithmic bias, manipulation, and limited explainability can affect decision quality, consumer autonomy, fairness, and access to redress. Drawing on national and international regulatory frameworks and practical cases involving ecommerce, facial recognition, algorithmic pricing, financial services, and automated advice, the study evaluates how technical and institutional controls can reduce decision risks. Attention is given to transparency, human oversight, data governance, accountability, liability allocation, and the ability of consumers to challenge consequential automated decisions. The article conceptualises regulation as a decision control mechanism that complements technical safeguards in AI enabled decision support systems. It further proposes a responsible AI decision governance perspective in which predictive performance is assessed alongside fairness, explainability, robustness, consumer autonomy, and accountability. The resulting framework connects computer based decision processes with economic decision making, organisational governance, and consumer protection, thereby supporting the design and deployment of more trustworthy AI assisted decision systems.

W7222892831.abstract: Fruit image analysis has become an essential research area in precision agriculture, enabling automated fruit classification, quality grading, maturity estimation, disease diagnosis, yield prediction, and intelligent harvesting through advances in computer vision and artificial intelligence (AI).Recent progress in imaging technologies, large-scale benchmark datasets, and deep learning has substantially improved the accuracy, robustness, and scalability of automated fruit analysis systems.This survey presents a comprehensive and systematic review of image processing and AI techniques for fruit image analysis.It covers the complete image analysis pipeline, including image acquisition, preprocessing, enhancement, color space transformation, segmentation, feature extraction, and handcrafted texture descriptors.Furthermore, conventional machine learning algorithms are reviewed alongside state-of-the-art deep learning architectures, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Vision Transformers (ViTs), and Vision Mamba models, for applications such as fruit recognition, quality assessment, disease detection, ripeness estimation, and object detection.Publicly available benchmark datasets, evaluation metrics, and performance comparison strategies are also summarized to facilitate objective assessment of existing approaches.In addition, the survey discusses key research challenges, including illumination variations, occlusion, complex orchard environments, limited annotated datasets, computational complexity, and domain adaptation, while highlighting emerging research trends such as self-supervised learning, multimodal learning, explainable AI, lightweight deep networks, foundation models, and edge intelligence for real-time deployment.By providing a unified review of methodologies, datasets, evaluation protocols, challenges, and future research directions, this survey offers a comprehensive reference for researchers and practitioners developing intelligent and scalable fruit image analysis systems for precision agriculture.

W7223021826.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a key method for training AI models in scientific applications, but RL remains difficult when outputs cannot easily be verified against a known ground-truth answer. Natural-language weather forecast reports are one such domain: they translate atmospheric data into assessments of weather evolution, hazards, and uncertainty for both the general public and key decision-makers. Unlike numerical weather-analysis questions, they admit many valid outputs, which limits deterministic verification. To address this, we develop Zephyrus-R1, a practical framework for RL on scientific weather forecast reporting. We focus on three key components of the agentic RL pipeline: reward design, curriculum learning, and an analysis of human-expert alignment. To encourage both report legibility and factual accuracy, we design a reward function that combines a meteorological rubric with bidirectional claim entailment, both evaluated against National Weather Service reference reports. Our framework optimizes this reward in a simulated tool-calling environment, enabling vision-language agents to gather and analyze forecast evidence across regions and lead times before producing a report. We use annotations from three meteorologists to audit the claim labels produced by our LLM judges. Finally, a curriculum helps small models first develop tool use and scientific reasoning through RL on verifiable weather-analysis questions, then optimize the open-ended report reward. After training Qwen3.5-4B with Zephyrus-R1, we improve the mean across six judge-metric scores by 26% over the base model and achieve results competitive with frontier open-weight models. For Qwen3.8-27B, we improve the same mean by 13% over the base model, by 6.7% over Kimi-K3, and by 2.7% over GPT-5.6-Luna.

W7223118347.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are enabling agents to move beyond predefined workflows toward autonomous planning and execution, creating new opportunities for smart manufacturing. However, dynamic environments, complex physical constraints, and stringent reliability requirements hinder the direct deployment of general-purpose agents in smart manufacturing. This article presents a systematic overview of LLM-driven industrial agents. First, we analyze five key challenges and discuss the concept and core characteristics of industrial agents. We then establish a unified taxonomy covering application scenarios, embodiment forms, and five capability levels. Next, we propose a four-layer system architecture and detail its core modules and operational mechanisms for closed-loop task execution. Finally, we review representative applications across the industrial lifecycle and outline future research directions. This article provides a structured reference for the design, development, and application of industrial agents.

W7223134151.abstract: Continuous flow language models offer a path to parallel generation with tools for control and acceleration unavailable to discrete diffusion, yet effective techniques for building them at the billion-parameter scale remain less established. We present Lafa (Large flow language model), a fast, high-performing flow language model scaled to 8B parameters in a data-efficient manner. Lafa is a blockwise flow model with causal attention on the prefix and bidirectional, asynchronous flow within each block. This design enables efficient training by adapting pretrained autoregressive (AR) models and fast inference via prefix caching and blockwise parallel decoding. We train Lafa at 0.5B, 7B, and 8B scales with fewer than 30B tokens, more efficient than previous diffusion models, and evaluate it on instruction following, reasoning, and coding, where the learned flow matches or surpasses the quality of AR and can be distilled into flow maps for one- and few-step generation. Notably, flow training preserves or even improves pretrained AR capabilities via a multi-token prediction effect, which we leverage in a self-speculative decoding scheme that verifies flow-based drafts autoregressively within a single model. This yields 2.54x the throughput of an AR model at comparable quality, outperforming multi-token prediction and discrete diffusion methods. Our findings show that continuous flows can serve as a scalable foundation for language modeling.

W7223159601.abstract: This paper investigates the feasibility of using autonomous AI agents to conduct Red Team evaluations of Large Language Models (LLMs) with minimal human supervision. We propose a framework of specialized agents targeting sensitive domains, including homicide, human trafficking, and zoophilia, which interact with aligned and less aligned LLMs to elicit and identify harmful outputs. The method aligns encouragingly with expert majority judgments, though the low inter-rater agreement highlights the subjectivity of harmfulness assessment, which we discuss as a central limitation. Overall, the framework shows potential as a scalable, cost-efficient support tool for LLM safety evaluation.

W7223178242.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative Agentic AI) models, such as Large Language Models (LLMs), and agentic AI have recently gained widespread attention in both research and industry. They have rapidly emerged as a concept that elevates Generative Agentic AI from passive text generators to the next generation of agentic AI as autonomous, goal-driven agents capable of perception, planning, and dynamic action execution—Coherent Generative Agentic AI (CGA). In addition, CGA provides supervisory intelligence by maintaining persistent, evolving internal world models of the environment, networks, resources, agents, user intents, and policies. CGA reasons over time, runs long-horizon plans, checks consequences against its internal models, and coherently orchestrates lower-level controllers. It sits above network controllers, providing a global, semantic, model-driven brain. The paper starts with a review of CGA functional and non-functional characteristics in the context of key research and development results of agentic AI. It introduces a coherence-first architectural construct and system variable across all future 6G/7G networking planes (data-, transport-, management and operations,- orchestration,- autonomicity-, programmability-, and AI_as_a_Service-plane). It proposes a new deterministic CGA mathematical (CGAM) model that provides a new abstraction and theoretical foundation for analyzing the systemic consequences of different structural design and optimization options. It defines the relation between coherence and intelligence. The CGAM model represents the compute–communications continuum as a partially observable, intent-driven, contract-governed, multi-agent dynamical system with persistent memory and coherence constraints. We also included detailed CGAM validation and evaluation measures. This paper explores and details the CGAM’s role in 6G and 7G networking, as well as the challenges and opportunities for future work they present. We present the CGA-enabled 6G networking as well as 7G networking. Our investigation maps the current development landscape and points to future research and development in using Generative Agentic AI for networking.

W7223261161.abstract: Text embedding and text generation are two of the most useful capabilities of modern large language models, yet they are typically provided by separate specialized models (an embedder and a generator) trained with incompatible objectives and deployed side by side in retrieval-augmented generation and agent systems. Recent unified embedding-generation models such as GritLM share parameters between the two capabilities, but they either switch attention regimes between modes or optimize embedding and language modeling as parallel objectives that never supervise each other. We argue that these designs are only partially unified: the two capabilities coexist on the same weights, but do not shape each other. We propose ULME, a post-training framework that unifies embedding and language modeling on a causal decoder-only LLM through predictive coupling. ULME inserts a chain of learnable slots between the query and the answer, reads a semantic embedding and a reasoning embedding from two designated slots, and trains three objectives on a shared causal backbone: a contrastive loss anchoring the semantic slot to document representations, a language-modeling loss supervising answer generation, and a stop-gradient predictive loss that aligns the reasoning slot with a pooled summary of the answer, so that generation actively shapes what the embedding encodes. Across two model families (Qwen2.5, Qwen3) and eight scales spanning 0.5B-8B parameters, a single ULME checkpoint improves MTEB by 3.3-4.1 points over the strongest open-source baseline, tightens BRIGHT and AdvBench-IR simultaneously, and remains on par with a generation-only fine-tune on standard accuracy benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, HumanEval), demonstrating that genuine unification yields mutually reinforcing rather than merely coexisting capabilities.

W7223693902.abstract: Understanding language-agent behaviour requires learning how actions are organised across a trajectory and how this organisation relates to context and outcomes. We propose a general framework that connects data-driven behavioural discovery with analysis and experimental investigation. Categories developed from recorded activity define what is measured. Analyses preserve the behaviours' positions in the process and express their relationships as interpretable hypotheses. Statistical assessment and tests in held-out contexts examine the strength and scope of the evidence. Experiments, including prompt steering, then test how behaviour and outcomes change under deliberately varied conditions. A study of iterative self-reflection illustrates how discovery, dependency learning and prompt comparisons can inform one another. We develop this approach for trajectories of varying length, event order and agent roles, and identify advances in coding, analysis and experimentation needed to support its wider use.

W7223790177.abstract: Semiconductor systems have become more complex with the advent of AI applications, especially those using AI chiplets at the highest technology nodes like 3 nm.The proliferation of AI applications has made semiconductor systems more complex, especially for AI chiplets at advanced technology nodes like 3 nm. The development time, cost of design and productivity in traditional RTL-to-GDSII design methodology is high because of the dependency on human expertise and iterative optimization. In recent years, the rise of Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) and foundation models offers a promising path to redefine semiconductor design automation, offering the capability of making autonomous decisions throughout various phases of the electronic design automation (EDA) process. A hierarchical multi-agent foundation model framework for the autonomous RTL-to-GDSII design of chiplet-based AI accelerator for the RISC-V architecture in 3 nm FinFET/GAAFET technology is presented. The proposed framework is an orchestration, hierarchical structure, composed of specialized agents for specification analysis, RTL generation, verification, design for test (DFT), physical design and timing closure. The floorplanning, placement, routing and congestion prediction are enhanced by AI-driven optimization techniques such as graph neural networks and reinforcement learning, and foundation models are used to convert natural language specifications into synthesizable Verilog/SystemVerilog descriptions. The proposed framework is evaluated using a case study of a chiplet-based RISC-V AI accelerator that consists of compute, memory, interconnect and security chiplets. The experimental validation is done with OpenROAD, OpenLane, Yosys, Vivado and FPGA emulation platforms. Results indicate that the proposed approach enables to save 6 weeks of RTL development time and 100% to 25% manual verification efforts. In addition, the 40% run-time reduction, 27% reduction in routing congestion and 3x faster convergence to timing closure provide a 38% improvement in power-performance-area (PPA) metrics that are achieved by the AI-assisted physical design flow. The results suggest a viable and scalable approach to achieving fully autonomous design of semiconductor devices at high technology nodes for future (UTeM) chiplet-based AI systems using hierarchical multi agent foundation models

W7223980335.abstract: Abstract Distorted cognitive behaviors significantly impair decision-making and mental well-being, highlighting the need for innovative methods for addressing negative thought patterns. This study introduces a framework for analyzing sentiment polarity in thought-related text, classifying textual expressions into positive and negative sentiments, with potential applications in computational mental health research. A large-scale dataset (n = 156,785) was curated by collecting and annotating social media texts, to capture both positive and negative sentiment polarity in thought-related expression. A comprehensive evaluation was conducted across various machine-learning (ML) models, from traditional classifiers to advanced transformer-based architectures. The study utilized the Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) and Bag-of-Words (BoW) feature representations, with 5-fold cross-validation for robustness. Among the traditional models, Logistic Regression (LR) and Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) achieved comparable performance, with BoW-based Logistic Regression yielding the highest accuracy of 92.87% ± 0.13% (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.927, 0.930). Among the transformer models, Distilled Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (DistilBERT) provided the best overall performance with an accuracy of 84.07% ± 0.15% (95% CI: 0.839–0.843), demonstrating stable precision-recall trade-offs across classes. In addition, a decoder-only language model (Llama-2) analysis achieved moderate classification performance with 80.20% ± 2.35% accuracy using instruction-based prompting. Overall, the findings demonstrate the effectiveness of lightweight machine learning models and distilled transformers for large-scale sentiment analysis of thought-related social media texts. Practically, the framework is positioned as a research-oriented tool that requires human oversight for future mental health-related applications.

W7224103967.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms have been observed to lose the ability to adaptively learn from new data, a phenomenon termed Loss of Plasticity (LoP). While many metrics have been shown to correlate with it, the causal mechanisms and the geometric conditions from which it can arise have not been clearly identified. We analyze LoP in Proximal Policy Optimization with isotropic Gaussian policies, the state-of-the-art formulation for many continuous action spaces in RL. We report multiple metrics which characterize the effect that the policy standard deviation $σ$ has on LoP, and we also suggest related explanations for the effectiveness of widely adopted LoP mitigation techniques. We observe a significant effect of $σ$ on the extent of LoP, and accompany this with both theoretical and experimental supporting arguments. Our experimental validation consists of LoP benchmark evaluations against standard baselines as well as real-world policy deployment on a 7-DoF robotic arm.

W7224115057.abstract: Introduction. Artificial intelligence (AI) in clinical practice refers to a set of digital analysis methods capable of performing tasks that typically require a physician's involvement. Unlike conventional medical software, AI algorithms process vast amounts of historical health data to identify patterns and apply them to analyze new data. Sought-after technologies in this field include machine learning, neural network-based deep learning (DL), and large language models (LLMs). Aim. To evaluate the potential and limitations of AI technologies in gastroenterological practice and to explore their contribution to the optimization and enhancement of the quality of clinical decision-making. Materials and methods . A literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE, eLIBRARY.RU, and Google Scholar databases was conducted for the period from 2021 to August 2026. A total of 204 papers were evaluated, and 97 were included in the review. The search terms were as follows: artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, neural networks, large language models, clinical practice, medical diagnostics, multi-criteria decision analysis, explainable artificial intelligence. A supplementary manual search of the reference lists of relevant reviews was conducted. Results. AI systems can analyze diagnostic images, predict disease outcomes, and computerize document processing. Algorithm training replicates clinical experience: the model can acquire differential diagnosis skills by analyzing endoscopic images. LLMs structure electronic health record (EHR) data and support differential diagnosis. MCDA takes into account patients’ quality of life, their individual characteristics, resource constraints, clinical priorities, and prognosis of the individual course of disease. At the same time, AI lacks clinical reasoning and causal reasoning capabilities; performance of AI models is determined by AI training data quality. Conclusion. AI technologies in healthcare serve as supportive tools for physicians that aid, rather than replace, the clinical reasoning of clinicians and other healthcare professionals. Mandatory validation of the scope and efficacy of AI solutions in accordance with established methodological and regulatory requirements will become a reliable basis for their integration into gastroenterologal practice and medical care standards.

W7224116846.abstract: Pruned language models are judged almost entirely by accuracy and perplexity, which assumes that preserved output behaviour implies preserved internal computation. We test this assumption with a factorial pruning study on GPT-2, crossing two importance criteria (magnitude, random), two component types (attention heads, MLP neurons) and three sparsity levels (3%, 50%, 70%). Using the fully characterised indirect object identification (IOI) circuit as ground truth, we measure circuit integrity with activation patching, path patching and direct logit attribution. We find two qualitatively distinct failure modes. Magnitude head pruning >= zeroes the circuit: output-facing heads are removed, and the model falls to near-chance. Magnitude neuron pruning at 30% inverts it: all 26 circuit heads remain intact, but Name Mover contributions flip sign, and the model systematically prefers the wrong name (17.7% accuracy). Perplexity ranks it as less damaged than random head pruning (74.6 vs 140.1). A replication of the Greater-Than circuit shows that the critical component type depends on the circuit's architecture. These results show that output metrics and structural checks can both miss mechanistic damage, motivating circuit-level causal analysis as a complementary evaluation of compressed language models.

W7224242533.abstract: We introduce SocialArena, a benchmark for systematically defining and evaluating the social intelligence of large language models (LLMs).Although LLMs are increasingly deployed in socially interactive applications such as mental health counseling, companionship chatbots, and educational tutoring, existing evaluations remain fragmented-focusing on isolated capabilities or single scenarios-and evaluation reliability is largely unverified.This work makes three main contributions to address these limitations.(1) We first propose a unified three-tier framework that defines social intelligence along three capability dimensions: role-playing ability, mental state reasoning, and behavioral reasoning.To operationalize this definition, we design a role-playing dialogue paradigm with explicit character thinking for evaluation, enabling simultaneous assessment of these capabilities in a manner that mirrors realistic human interactions.(2) To ensure diversity across social scenarios and thereby prevent evaluation conclusions from being confined to specific scenarios, we introduce the U-TRIMF framework, which guides us in synthesizing social contexts with broad coverage.(3) To obtain reliable evaluation, we invest $132.4K to recruit and train human annotators and adopt a human-annotated arena-style protocol, where annotators compare model responses and provide preference labels along with natural-language critiques.We hope that SocialArena can provide valuable insights and guidance for future LLM improvements.

W7224654929.abstract: Reliable evaluation of factual recall in large language models (LLMs) requires ground truth that is broad, clean, and complete.Yet existing benchmarks often rely on narrow domains or incomplete knowledge bases that penalise models for generating correct facts absent from the reference.We introduce MUSART, a benchmark of 21,775 subject-relation questions over 11 domains, created via a schema-free extraction pipeline that can be cheaply regenerated from public dumps.To overcome knowledgebase incompleteness, we contribute a sourcegrounded augmentation pipeline that mines verifiable facts directly from article text.Evaluating twenty-one open-weight LLMs against a dual-reference pair (original vs. augmented) yields three findings: (i) completeness correction systematically raises precision and lowers recall across all models; (ii) factual recall varies widely across subject domains, demonstrating that single-domain evaluation confounds model capability with subject matter; and (iii) the precision gap between the two references separates instances where models lack knowledge from instances where the knowledge base lacks facts, proving that completeness-blind evaluation penalises both identically.All code, data, and evaluation scripts are publicly released at https://github.com/Rajjaa/MUSART.

W7224791229.abstract: An autonomous research laboratory could conduct an entire study, from formulating questions to preparing manuscripts. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers one route towards this goal. Recent AI systems take on several research roles, but may draw conclusions that the evidence does not support. Here, we present an autonomous research laboratory in which agents based on large language models assess one another's work and can stop or redirect investigations. They can generate and reject research questions, require separate theoretical checks and conduct experiments designed to challenge their claims. We demonstrate these capabilities by investigating ensembles of quantum spins in diamond. The agents derived the minimum number of calibration settings needed to predict responses to a defined family of microwave pulse sequences. They checked the result computationally and designed experiments to distinguish competing predictions. An initial experiment agreed with the theoretical predictions, but repeated reference measurements showed that the signal was drifting during data collection. The agents therefore treated the result as inconclusive and revised the measurement protocol without relaxing the acceptance criteria. The revised experiment met those criteria and supported the theoretical predictions. This study demonstrates that collaborating AI agents can select research questions, derive theoretical results and test their predictions experimentally.

W7224907701.abstract: Clinical text summarization has emerged as an important application of Natural Language Processing (NLP) to efficiently summarize the rapidly growing volume of Electronic Health Records (EHRs) and other medical documents. This survey reviews recent advancements in clinical text summarization by analyzing twenty representative studies that employ transformer-based models, Large Language Models (LLMs), hybrid approaches, semantic graph techniques, multimodal learning, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). The survey compares widely used models, including Bidirectional and Auto-Regressive Transformers (BART), Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer(T5), Pre-training with Extracted Gap-sentences for Abstractive Summarization(PEGASUS), Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers for Biomedical Text Mining (BioBERT), Clinical Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers(ClinicalBERT), Generative Pre-trained Transformer(GPT), and Large Language Model Meta AI (LLaMA), based on their methodologies, performance, strengths, limitations, and evaluation metrics. The analysis indicates that transformer-based and hybrid models produce more coherent, context-aware, and clinically relevant summaries than traditional extractive methods; however, challenges such as factual hallucination, limited explainability, privacy concerns, computational complexity, and the lack of standardized evaluation datasets continue to hinder their practical adoption. Based on these findings, the survey identifies key research gaps and highlights future research directions toward developing accurate, explainable, multimodal, and clinically reliable clinical text summarization systems to support efficient healthcare decision-making and improve patient care.

W7225062460.abstract: Integrated circuits (ICs) have played a fundamental role in the development of modern electronics, computing, and information technologies. This review presents an overview of the historical evolution of IC technology, from the invention of the transistor and the first integrated circuits to the emergence of very-large-scale integration, advanced complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) technologies, and nanoscale semiconductor devices. Particular attention is given to the physical principles of semiconductor integration, transistor scaling, lithographic techniques, and advances in semiconductor materials. Major technological milestones, including the development of microprocessors, system-on-chip architectures, three-dimensional integration, and chiplet-based designs, are discussed. Applications in computing, telecommunications, artificial intelligence, automotive electronics, and industrial systems are highlighted. Furthermore, challenges associated with power consumption, thermal management, fabrication complexity, and physical scaling limitations are examined. Emerging technologies and future research directions are discussed to provide a comprehensive perspective on the continued evolution of integrated circuits.

W7225095053.abstract: Academic program analysis plays a critical role in supporting curriculum design, academic advising, and student decision-making. However, most curriculum frameworks are provided in semi-structured textual formats, where relationships among knowledge blocks, courses, learning outcomes, and prerequisite structures remain implicit and difficult to analyze systematically. This limitation hinders the ability of stakeholders to gain insights into curriculum structure, such as knowledge coverage, learning pathways, and graduation requirements. This paper proposes a knowledge graph reasoning framework for syllabi analysis, integrating Large Language Model (LLM)-based structured extraction with graph-based modeling and reasoning techniques. A curriculum knowledge model is first defined to represent academic programs. A semi-automated data pipeline is then developed to extract structured information from curriculum documents and construct a knowledge graph in Neo4j. On top of this graph, a reasoning engine is designed to support query-based and rule-based analysis, enabling stakeholders to explore curriculum structures and answer practical questions. The framework is validated using real-world curriculum data from a university program. The findings highlight the potential of combining LLM-based extraction with knowledge graph reasoning for scalable and insightful curriculum analytics.

W7225148783.abstract: Knowledge is how understanding accumulates across people and generations: durable records that outlive their producers and that others can check, combine, teach, and correct. AI agents are now built and run by many independent users and organizations, and each agent is upgraded, replaced, or retired within months. Yet what an agent learns stays trapped in model parameters, a transient context window, or a system-specific memory store that is appended to and retrieved from rather than processed. We argue that the next generation of AI should be knowledge-centric, built around an explicit, continuously evolving knowledge layer independent of any single agent. In this loop, agents discover knowledge from their environments and trajectories; the layer internalizes it by turning fragmented, heterogeneous records and experience into composable, revisable understanding; and agents across systems and generations use the result and return new outcomes for revision. While discovery and use have advanced rapidly with large language model agents, internalization remains the bottleneck. We argue that internalization should become a persistent object of training and maintenance-centered on condition-preserving conceptualization of events and deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning across noisy, heterogeneous representations (text, tables, graphs, rules, and programs). To power this layer, we call for knowledge foundation models that provide shared neural capacity for knowledge computation, and outline a research agenda showing how an explicit knowledge layer delivers reuse, cost efficiency, auditability, and continuity across agent generations.

W7225225918.abstract: Background: Natural products remain an important source of therapeutic agents, but their discovery is constrained by chemical complexity, time-consuming isolation, difficult structure elucidation, and high attrition rates. Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning, deep learning, graph neural networks, and generative AI, offers computational approaches to address these challenges. Method: This narrative review examines peer-reviewed, English-language literature published between 2021 and 2026, retrieved from PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar. The selected literature was analyzed using thematic qualitative synthesis to identify AI applications, reported contributions, and persistent limitations across the natural product discovery pipeline. Problem Identification: Despite growing interest in AI-assisted drug discovery, the extent to which current methods address the limitations of conventional approaches remains uncertain. Key concerns include data quality, model reliability, interpretability, and the need for experimental validation. Results: AI applications cover target identification, biosynthetic gene cluster mining, virtual screening, structure elucidation, network pharmacology, generative molecular design, and absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) prediction. These methods can help prioritize candidate compounds and predict potential biological activities. However, data scarcity and bias, inconsistent evaluation practices, limited interpretability, and insufficient experimental validation remain significant barriers. Explainable AI, multi-omics integration, and self-driving laboratories represent promising developments, although their practical contributions require further validation. Conclusion: AI can support and accelerate selected stages of natural product-based drug discovery but cannot replace experimental testing or the expertise of natural product chemists and pharmacologists.

W7225271207.abstract: Solid electrolytes are widely expected to replace flammable liquid electrolytes in lithium batteries, yet cell-level progress has lagged behind the large gains in bulk ionic conductivity achieved over the past decade. This review argues that the electrode–electrolyte interface, rather than the bulk electrolyte, should be the unit of design, and examines the consequences of this view for engineering practice and for artificial intelligence (AI)-guided discovery. Using a documented, non-systematic literature selection (mainly 2018–2026, with earlier foundational work), we first re-examine the safety premise: removing the liquid removes one fuel, but thermal-runaway pathways remain through cathode oxygen release, lithium-metal reactivity, and stored electrical energy. We then compare oxide, sulfide, halide/oxyhalide, solid polymer, gel/quasi-solid, and composite electrolytes, together with the cathodes and anodes they must contact, explain how solid–solid interfaces form and degrade chemically, electrochemically, and mechanically, and critically assess the experimental techniques used to diagnose them. An area-specific resistance analysis indicates that once separators are about 30 µm thick and conductivities exceed ∼1 mS cm⁻¹, interfacial and composite-electrode resistances, rather than bulk conductivity, usually dominate ohmic loss. Three ‘translation gaps’ are identified in which bulk metrics or computational descriptors (ionic conductivity, thermodynamic stability windows and elastic-modulus criteria) fail to predict cell behaviour. AI studies are graded on two complementary scales: the type of validation (Levels L1–L4) and the cell-level validation scale (grades A–D). Experimentally validated successes are concentrated in bulk properties and low-dimensional synthesis optimisation, whereas interface prediction remains largely computational, trained on small datasets and bounded by an experimental ‘noise floor’ (inter-laboratory relative standard deviations of 35–50% in the conductivity of identical samples). We propose an Interface Co-Design Framework with four operationally defined validity gates, chemical pairing, mechanical contact, transport translation, and manufacturing and safety validation, together with measurable reporting criteria and a Minimum Interface Data Record. AI is likely to accelerate practical solid-state batteries only if its training labels describe the failure modes that limit cells and if electrolyte, electrode, interface and processing are optimised jointly rather than sequentially.

W7225297620.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly reshaping software engineering (SE) across the development lifecycle. This review synthesises 113 peer-reviewed journal studies and organises the literature around five research questions and four application areas: code generation, testing and debugging, human–AI collaboration, and quality assurance. The reviewed studies show substantial progress in natural-language-to-code generation, context-aware programming, automated testing, fault localisation, program repair, and AI-assisted development. At the same time, persistent challenges remain in semantic correctness, non-deterministic outputs, software security, maintainability, verification, and evaluation consistency. Drawing these findings together, the paper presents a lifecycle mapping, a closed-loop AI-driven software engineering framework, and a four-dimension taxonomy to organise existing research and clarify connections across previously fragmented areas. Overall, generative AI is moving software engineering from a largely deterministic and human-centred workflow toward a more probabilistic and AI-enhanced engineering process. Further progress will depend on stronger verification, security, reliability, maintainability, and appropriately calibrated human oversight.

W7225330753.abstract: Materials discovery increasingly depends on a multiscale ecosystem of simulations, experiments, and shared facilities, yet advances in individual AI tools do not by themselves connect the decisions that link these components. This gap is especially severe in all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs), whose development couples electrochemical performance to interfacial stability, mechanics, processing, manufacturability, reliability, safety, and cost. Here we argue that AI agents could support ASSB development toward commercial viability by maintaining a shared decision–evidence state that links materials discovery and optimization to cell-level validation and manufacturing constraints. We develop this argument through three complementary dimensions of scientific agency: coordination across heterogeneous resources, method augmentation across models and scales, and project-level adaptation over time. Cross-domain demonstrations establish several relevant capability primitives, including stateful tool planning, task execution, and delegated analysis. Agents should therefore be evaluated as supporting infrastructure for concurrent ASSB engineering rather than as autonomous replacements for scientific expertise. Their value ultimately lies in driving materials development in the context of interfaces, cell architectures, and manufacturing processes toward the performance, reliability, safety, and cost requirements of ASSB commercialization. context & scale Commercializing all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) requires more than identifying high-performing materials: ion transport, interphase chemistry, mechanics, processing, cell architecture, reliability, safety, and cost impose coupled constraints that can invalidate otherwise promising candidates. This Perspective argues that AI agents could serve as auditable infrastructure, maintaining a decision-evidence state that connects objectives, specimen histories, models, uncertainties, actions, and validation to support ASSB development. Such infrastructure could broaden research across instruments and engineering stages, strengthen validation by linking atomistic, mesoscale, continuum, and experimental descriptions, and preserve evidence and revisions throughout development cycles. Future efforts should move beyond task-level demonstrations toward systematic ASSB development, establishing whether agents can contribute to the development of reliable and economically viable ASSB systems.

W7225342750.abstract: Introduction Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is one of the greatest global public health threats, contributing to an estimated 4.95 million deaths annually worldwide (Murray et al., 2022). AMR is driven by inappropriate antimicrobial use in human medicine, veterinary practice, agriculture, and environmental contamination. The One Health approach, integrating human, animal, and environmental health, provides a comprehensive framework for addressing AMR. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers promising opportunities to strengthen AMR surveillance and antimicrobial stewardship (WHO, 2023). To systematically review applications of AI technologies in AMR surveillance, prediction, diagnosis, prevention, management, and antimicrobial discovery across human, animal, and environmental health sectors. Methods A systematic review was conducted following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews (PRISMA 2020) guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and IEEE Xplore were searched for studies published from January 2015 to March 2026. Search terms included “artificial intelligence,” “machine learning,” “deep learning,” “predictive analytics,” “antimicrobial resistance,” “antibiotic resistance,” and “One Health.” Eligible studies evaluated AI applications for AMR surveillance, diagnostics, antimicrobial stewardship, resistance prediction, or antimicrobial discovery in human, veterinary, agricultural, or environmental settings. Results The search identified 2,146 records, of which 58 studies met the inclusion criteria. Of these, 20 (34.5%) focused on AMR surveillance, 16 (27.6%) on predictive modelling, 13 (22.4%) on rapid diagnostics, and 9 (15.5%) on antimicrobial discovery. AI-assisted diagnostic platforms reduced the time required for pathogen identification and susceptibility testing compared with conventional laboratory methods. Conclusion AI demonstrates substantial potential to transform the global response to AMR. Across One Health sectors, AI can strengthen surveillance, improve antimicrobial stewardship, accelerate diagnostics, predict resistance patterns, and support discovery of novel antimicrobial agents.
